The 2-Vial presentation was stored as separate antigen component and adjuvant component vials. Immediately prior to use, the lyophilized antigen vial was reconstituted with water and 40 muL antigen was mixed with 460 muL 20% w/v sucrose diluent and 500 muL of adjuvant, which results in the same antigen and adjuvant concentrations as the single-vial presentations in Table 1.
Not applicable.

POC, TT, TP, and SP formulations were prepared by combining concentrated stock solutions of ID93, GLA-SE, and buffered excipients to final concentrations of 4 mug/mL ID93, 10 mug/mL GLA, and 2% v/v squalene, with excipient and buffer content as listed in Table 1. Sterile 3-mL 13-mm Ready-to-Fill glass vials (Afton Scientific, Charlottesville, VA) were filled with 1 mL of formulation, partially stoppered with 2-leg chlorobutyl Wheaton lyophilization stoppers (DWK Life Sciences, Staffordshire, UK), and placed into the lyophilization chamber. The POC formulation vials were lyophilized at AAHI in a VirTis AdVantage 2.0 EL-85 benchtop freeze dryer (SP Scientific, Warminster, PA). The POC lyophilization cycle was essentially as described previously, consisting of an equilibration step at 4  C, freezing at -40  C, annealing at -15  C, primary drying at -20  C and 100 mTorr, and secondary drying at 25  C and 50-100 mTorr. Samples were then blanketed with high-purity nitrogen and stoppered at 500 mTorr prior to being removed from the lyophilization chamber. TT, TP, and SP were lyophilized at LTI in an 8FS12C freeze dryer (SP Hull, Warminster, PA). The cycle consisted of an equilibration step at 5  C, freezing at -40  C, primary drying at -33  C and 50 mTorr, and secondary drying at 25  C and 50 mTorr, followed by stoppering under nitrogen at 14.7 psia. All vials were crimped and stored at 4  C until samples were placed in stability monitoring chambers at 4  C, 37  C, or 50  C.

The antigen component of the 2-Vial formulation was prepared at 100 mug/mL ID93 in 4% w/v mannitol, 1% w/v sucrose, and 0.1% w/v polysorbate 80 in 20 mM Tris pH 8.0 and was lyophilized using a process slightly modified from the POC cycle (above) including a slower freezing ramp rate, a longer freezing hold time at -40  C, and less annealing time at -15  C. The adjuvant component of the 2-Vial formulation was prepared by diluting concentrated stock GLA-SE to 20 mug/mL GLA, 4% v/v squalene, 7.6 mg/mL dimyristoyl phosphatidylcholine (DMPC), 0.036 mg/mL poloxamer 188, and 9.2 mg/mL glycerol in 25 mM ammonium phosphate buffer. To prepare the mixed 2-Vial formulation, 40 muL of the reconstituted antigen component was mixed with 460 muL of 20% w/v sucrose diluent and 500 muL of the adjuvant component. The single-vial Liq formulation was prepared by mixing ID93, GLA-SE, and Tris buffer at the concentrations described in Table 1. Liquid formulations were filled at 1-mL volume into 3-mL 13-mm Ready-to-Fill glass vials, stoppered, crimped, and stored at 4  C no more than 1 week before being placed in stability monitoring chambers.
Short-term stress test conditions

All samples were removed from 4  C storage, equilibrated to ambient temperature, and visually inspected for their physical appearance and container integrity before initiating stability testing at AAHI. For all tests, two vials per formulation were tested under stressed conditions and two additional vials per formulation were placed in a control condition for comparison.
Mechanical stress

Formulation vials were placed in a cryobox with appropriately sized dividers to hold the vials upright and attached to a KS 260 benchtop orbital shaker with an AS 260.1 top plate (IKA Works, Wilmington, NC). Vials underwent shaking at 350 rpm at ambient temperature for 1 week. Control samples were placed in a cryobox on the benchtop next to the shaker for 1 week.
Photochemical stress

Exposure to controlled light conditions was conducted at the University of Iowa Pharmaceuticals (Iowa City, IA). Formulation vials were placed in a photostability chamber and stressed according to International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) guidelines with 1.2 million lux hours of visible light and 200 W h/m2 of UV light. The total exposure time was 21.8 h at 27  C. Control vials were wrapped in aluminum foil and stored within the same chamber.
Oxidative stress

The aluminum crimp seals and vial stoppers were removed from selected vials, and the unstoppered vials were equilibrated to ambient temperature for 30 min and then placed in an incubator set at 50  C for 1 month. Control vials were kept under the same conditions (i.e., in the incubator) but remained stoppered. The 2-Vial formulation was not included in this test since evaporation would have confounded results.
Freeze-thaw stress

Formulation vials were cycled between -20  C and 25  C for a total of five cycles. In each case, storage time at -20  C was at least 24 h and storage time at 25  C was 30 min. Control vials were stored at 4  C.
Storage after reconstitution

Lyophilized formulation vials were reconstituted with 1 mL of ultrapure water. In the case of the 2-Vial formulation, the antigen and adjuvant components were mixed immediately before testing. Vials were stoppered, and samples were placed at 25  C for 1 week. Non-reconstituted control vials were placed in the same incubator for 1 week and then reconstituted immediately before the time of analysis.
Analytical characterization methods
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)

SEM imaging was performed by Micron Inc. (Wilmington, DE). Lyophilized cakes were extracted from the vials by scribing and breaking the vials. Once removed, the cakes were fractured, placed on a gold-coated carbon planchet with double-sided tape, and imaged with a JSM-6480 scanning electron microscope (JEOL, Peabody, MA) at 10-3,000x magnification.
Reconstitution time

To reconstitute lyophilized samples prior to analytical characterization, 1 mL of ultrapure water was added to the vial and the vial was swirled until the lyophilized cake was fully dissolved. A timer was used to measure the time required to fully dissolve the cake, based on visual assessment, in 5-s increments. If multiple vials were reconstituted for a sample, the average reconstitution time of the vials was reported.
Cryogenic transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM)

Cryo-TEM imaging was performed by NanoImaging Services (San Diego, CA). Following reconstitution, each sample was prepared by applying a 3-muL drop of sample to a clean holey carbon film on a 400-mesh copper grid, blotting away with filter paper, and vitrifying in liquid ethane. Prepared grids were stored in liquid nitrogen until transferred to a Tecnai T12 transmission electron microscope (FEI, Hillsboro, OR) operating at 120 keV and equipped with an Eagle 4k x 4k CCD camera (FEI). A cryostage maintained the prepared grids at <= -170  C. Images were collected at 21,000-110,000x magnification at a nominal underfocus of -5 to -2 mum and electron doses of ~10-20 e-/A2.
pH

The pH of the stored formulations after reconstitution at each time point was measured using an Orion ROSS Ultra Semi-micro pH Electrode (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) using an aliquot >=100 muL for each sample. Unless otherwise noted, pH measurements of the reconstituted samples were performed on one vial of each formulation at each time point.
Particle size

Average hydrodynamic diameter (Z-ave) was measured using dynamic light scattering (DLS) with a Zetasizer Nano S, Nano ZS, or APS (Malvern Panalytical, Malvern, UK) as previously described. One replicate of each sample was diluted 10-fold in freshly dispensed Milli-Q water (MilliporeSigma, Burlington, MA) and measured three times. Reported values are the average and standard deviation of all three measurements.
GLA content

GLA concentration was measured by reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC) using a C18 Atlantis T3 reversed-phase column (Waters, Milford, MA) with a methanol-chloroform gradient. Mobile phase A was 75:15:10 (v/v/v) methanol:chloroform:water containing 1% v/v acetic acid and 20 mM ammonium acetate. Mobile phase B contained 50:50 (v/v) methanol:chloroform, 1% v/v acetic acid, and 20 mM ammonium acetate. Duplicates of each sample were diluted 10-fold in mobile phase B prior to injection. Column temperature was held constant at 30  C, and GLA was detected with a Corona Charged Aerosol Detector (CAD) (ESA Biosciences, Chelmsford, MA). A standard curve was prepared from a GLA stock diluted in mobile phase B. The peak areas or heights from the standards were fit with a second-order polynomial per the CAD manufacturer's directions, and sample analyte concentrations were calculated by interpolation from the standard curve.
ID93 content

ID93 concentration was measured similarly to the previously described method by RP-HPLC with an Agilent 1100 series HPLC equipped with a fluorescence detector (Santa Clara, CA) and a Waters (Milford, MA) XBridge Protein BEH C4, 300 A analytical column (4.6 mm x 150 mm, 3.5 mum). Temperature was held at 60  C. Mobile phase A was 0.1% TEA in water (0.2 mum-filtered), and mobile phase B was 0.1% TEA in HPLC-grade acetonitrile. The method was run with linear gradient at 1.2 mL/min: 0-30 min, 2% B to 80% B; 30-31 min, 80% B to 2% B; 31-35 min, 2% B. All samples and standards were prepared in duplicate with 1% w/v SDS and 0.5% w/v beta-mercaptoethanol (BME). Fluorescence emission intensity was collected at 350 nm with excitation at 280 nm. Concentration of ID93 was determined by interpolation from a standard curve of ID93 peak area as a function of concentration.

Reducing sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) was used to detect the presence of the ID93 protein in reconstituted samples. Samples were mixed with 4x LDS reducing buffer containing 5% BME, heated to 90  C for 15 min, cooled, spun down, briefly vortexed, and then 24 ng of ID93 was loaded into a Tris-glycine 4-20% gradient gel. An ID93 control and a freshly admixed (i.e., non-lyophilized) ID93 + GLA-SE control were included for comparison (C1 and C2, respectively). Gels were run at 180 V for 65 min using Tris-glycine SDS running buffer and stained using a protein silver-staining kit (ProteoSilver, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) according to manufacturer's instructions. Stained gels were imaged using a gel imaging system (AlphaImager EC, ProteinSimple, San Jose, CA).
Long-term thermostability monitoring

Formulation vials were stored at 4  C, 37  C, and 50  C and monitored for up to 58 months. At each time point, single vials were pulled from each condition and characterized for particle size, GLA content, ID93 content, and pH.
Protective efficacy against Mtb aerosol challenge

All animal experiments were performed in accordance with national (NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals) and institutional guidelines for animal care of laboratory animals and approved by the IDRI Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC Protocol #2014/9). C57BL/6 mice (10 per group) were immunized intramuscularly with 100 muL vaccine formulation that had been stored at 4  C, 37  C, or 50  C for up to 3 months. Animals were immunized on Study Day 0 and Study Day 21. On Study Day 50, the mice were exposed to a low dose (50-100 colony-forming units [CFUs]/animal) of aerosolized Mtb (strain H37Rv). On Study Day 78, the mice were euthanized and the bacterial burdens were determined in the spleen and lung by serial dilution and plating on 7H10 plates (Middlebrook, Molecular Toxicology, Boone, NC) which were incubated at 37  C for 17 days prior to counting. Each experiment was repeated to ensure reproducibility of results.
Statistical methods

Protective efficacy outliers were removed using Grubbs' test. Reductions in log10 CFUs were tested for normality by the D'Agostino-Pearson test. Normally distributed data were also assessed for equality of group variances using the Brown-Forsythe test. Normally distributed data with equal group variances were evaluated by one-way ordinary ANOVA with Sidak's correction for multiple comparisons. Normally distributed data with unequal group variances were evaluated by one-way Welch's ANOVA with Dunnett's T3 correction for multiple comparisons. Datasets containing groups that failed the normality test were evaluated by the non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's correction for multiple comparisons. In all cases, the multiple selected pairwise comparisons included the following: unvaccinated vs. all vaccine formulations, 2-Vial vs. three lead candidate formulations (heat-stressed), 2-Vial (heat-stressed) vs. three lead candidate formulations (heat-stressed), Liq (heat-stressed) vs. three lead candidate formulations (heat-stressed), and POC (heat-stressed) vs. three lead candidate formulations (heat-stressed). Regarding the statistical analysis of selected physicochemical stability readouts, two-way ANOVA was employed with the two factors being formulation and stability assay, and Tukey's correction was applied for multiple comparisons. For all tests, p-values of <0.05 were considered significant.
Results
Formulation composition and morphology

Visual appearance of three lead candidate and three control formulations of ID93 + GLA-SE. Lead candidate single-vial lyophilized formulations: (A) TP, (B) TT, and (C) SP. Control formulations: (D) single-vial lyophilized POC, (E) 2-Vial consisting of lyophilized antigen component vial (left) and liquid adjuvant component vial (right), and (F) single-vial liquid Liq.
Fig. 1

Three lead candidate single-vial lyophilized ID93 + GLA-SE formulations (SP, TP, and TT) selected as described previously and three control formulations (Liq, POC, and 2-Vial) were prepared for physicochemical stability and protective efficacy evaluation (Table 1). Excipient differences between control and lead candidate formulations included antioxidant, tonicity, and/or buffer agents (Table 1). The visual observation results for the three lead candidate single-vial lyophilized formulations (TP, TT, and SP) were pharmaceutically elegant dried cakes with a uniform, dense, white appearance (Fig. 1A-C). The macro-structures were consistent with slight evidence of minor micro-collapse and/or shrinkage in some cases. In contrast, substantial shrinkage was evident in the POC formulation (Fig. 1D) as previously reported. Liquid control formulations containing GLA-SE (Liq and 2-Vial adjuvant component) appeared as milky-white emulsions (Fig. 1E and F).

SEM of the center of fractured lyophilized cakes from ID93 + GLA-SE formulations. Lead candidate single-vial formulations: (A) TP, (B) TT, and (C) SP. Control formulations: (D) single-vial POC and (E) antigen component of 2-Vial. Images taken at 300x magnification. Scale bar = 50 mum.
Fig. 2

The SEM imaging of the lead candidate lyophilized formulations (TP, TT, and SP), the POC formulation, and the antigen component of the 2-Vial formulation revealed some significant differences in microstructure. Some cracking of the dried material is also evident, though this may be associated with fracturing the cake during preparation of the sample for the SEM study. The SEM imaging indicated that the lead candidate formulations had an organized pore structure with primarily 3-point angular intersections of draping sheets of the solid solutes (Fig. 2A-C), characteristic of the impression for an amorphous composition left by formation and growth of irregularly sized ice crystals formed during freezing and subsequently sublimated during primary drying. The TP sample had the most ordered and elegant structure with angular intersections and very little rounding of the edges. The TT appeared similar to the TP formulation, with some evidence of rounded voids appearing within the sheets. The SP structure showed slightly thicker draping sheets with slight rounding and smaller or less open pore structures, suggesting a minor amount of micro-collapse associated with shrinkage. The POC sample had disorganized, irregularly sized and shaped strands and rounded structures (Fig. 2D), which suggests more extensive collapse than what was apparent in the TP, TT, and SP material, and was consistent with the shrunken macro-appearance of the lyophilized POC cake. The antigen component of the 2-Vial formulation appeared as plates, with some clusters emanating from a central point (Fig. 2E). The plates were generally flat with feathered edges and exhibited a repeating structure similar to rays emanating in a circle from a central point. Appearance of the structure suggests crystalline or partially crystalline morphology. Overall, the TP formulation exhibited the most elegant morphology, but all three lead candidates demonstrated acceptable dried structure.

Cryo-TEM of reconstituted lyophilized and non-lyophilized formulations of ID93 + GLA-SE. Lyophilized single-vial formulations: (A) TP, (B) TT, (C) SP, and (D) POC. (E) 2-Vial formulation mixture (including non-lyophilized adjuvant component and lyophilized antigen component). Images taken at 110,000x magnification. Scale bar = 100 nm.
Fig. 3

Physicochemical thermostability monitoring of ID93 + GLA-SE formulations stored at various temperatures for up to 58 months. Vaccine formulations include three lead candidates (TP, TT, and SP) and three controls (POC, 2-Vial, and Liq). (A) Particle size by DLS, (B) GLA concentration by HPLC-CAD, (C) ID93 concentration by HPLC-FLD, and (D) pH.
Fig. 4

Cryo-TEM imaging of the reconstituted lyophilized lead candidate and POC formulations revealed spherical oil droplets that were approximately 100 nm in diameter (Fig. 3A-D). This emulsion droplet morphology was highly similar to the appearance of the non-lyophilized 2-Vial formulation (Fig. 3E). Moreover, the ~100 nm droplet size was consistent with DLS results (Fig. 4). Notably, DLS data indicated a slight increase in particle diameter upon lyophilization and subsequent reconstitution compared to non-lyophilized liquid formulation (Fig. 4A). Overall, reconstituted emulsion droplet morphology did not appear to be substantially affected by lyophilization or by the excipient compositions employed for all lyophilized formulations tested (lead candidates and POC).

Five short-term stressed stability tests (mechanical, photochemical, oxidative, freeze-thaw, and storage after reconstitution) were performed on the TT, TP, SP, POC, and 2-Vial presentations to simulate alternative stresses that vaccine formulations could potentially encounter across various shipping, storage, and use conditions. The various test and control conditions are summarized in Table 2. The effects of the various stress conditions on formulation characteristics including visual appearance, reconstitution time, pH, particle diameter, GLA content, and ID93 content are summarized in Table 3. The difference between the stressed and control samples are reported as percent change. Regarding mechanical stress performance, minor cake shrinkage occurred in TP and POC, and up to 21% loss in GLA content (TP) was measured. Photochemical stress resulted in greater porosity in the POC cake, up to 20% loss in GLA content (2-Vial), and up to 100% loss in ID93 content (2-Vial). The oxidative stress test caused substantial cake shrinkage and increased reconstitution times in SP and POC, a 16% increase in particle size in POC, up to 25% loss in GLA content (TT), and up to 45% loss in ID93 content (TP). We note that the 2-Vial formulation control was not included in the oxidative stability test due to confounding evaporation effects. Regarding stability after freeze-thaw cycling, the 2-Vial presentation increased 15% in particle size, and up to 14% of ID93 content was lost (POC). Stability measured 1 week after reconstitution revealed the primary liability for all formulations to be ID93 content, with up to 100% loss (TP). Taken together, the most significant changes resulting from the short-term stress stability testing occurred in GLA content and ID93 content. Among the three lead candidate formulations, no single top performer was identified in the stressed stability testing. However, TP appeared to be most susceptible to ID93 content loss, TT tended to show the highest level of GLA content loss, and SP was the only lead formulation to show a change in cake appearance and reconstitution time. The three lead candidate formulations were generally more stable than the control formulations in the photochemical and freeze-thaw stress tests, but the 2-Vial presentation was the top performer in the mechanical stress test (wherein both vials were exposed to the mechanical stress). Statistical analysis confirmed that the three lead candidates significantly increased photochemical stability compared to the 2-Vial control by preserving ID93, TP was significantly less stable than the other two lead candidates regarding ID93 content following oxidative or reconstitution stress, and TT was less stable than the other two lead candidates regarding ID93 content following photochemical stress (Supplementary Table 1).
Long-term thermostability evaluation

To assess the long-term thermostability of the three lead candidate formulations and the three control formulations, formulation vials were stored at 4  C, 37  C, and 50  C and monitored for up to 58 months. At each time point, single vials were pulled from each condition and characterized for particle size, GLA content, ID93 content, and pH. Little or no change in particle size occurred in samples stored at 4  C, whereas particle size increased at elevated temperatures for all formulations but particularly for the control formulations (POC, 2-Vial, and Liq) (Fig. 4A). Among the three lead lyophilized formulations, TT was remarkably stable at elevated temperatures. GLA content was generally stable in all formulations at 4  C but rapidly declined in the control formulations (POC, 2-Vial, and Liq) at elevated temperatures (Fig. 4B). A slower rate of GLA content loss was apparent for the three lead lyophilized formulations, particularly for TP and TT, although no formulation had detectable GLA remaining after the 38-month time point when stored at 50  C. The analytical challenge associated with measuring a small amount of protein in a complex background matrix was apparent in the high level of variation in the measured ID93 content (Fig. 4C). Nevertheless, except for the single-vial liquid control (Liq), ID93 content generally appeared to remain stable at 4  C. At elevated temperatures, TP demonstrated greater rate of ID93 loss than the other lead formulations (TT and SP) and POC. TT maintained the highest ID93 content at 50  C at the 58-month time point. The ID93 HPLC-FLD results were consistent with SDS-PAGE band densities (Supplementary Fig. 1). The lyophilized formulations maintained pH at all temperatures for 58 months, except for the 50  C condition where <0.5 unit change occurred (Fig. 4D). In contrast, the 2-Vial and Liq pH values dropped >1 unit after 12 months at 50  C. Overall, TT appeared to be the most stable formulation during long-term storage at elevated temperatures. Indeed, statistical analysis confirmed that TT significantly increased thermal physical stability compared to the other two lead candidates, whereas all three lead candidates increased chemical stability compared to the 2-Vial control (Supplementary Table 1).
Protective efficacy against Mtb aerosol challenge

Protective efficacy of heat-stressed vaccine formulations of ID93 + GLA-SE against Mtb challenge. Reduction in CFUs in the (A) lungs and (B) spleens of mice immunized with lead candidate vaccine formulations (TP, TT, and SP) stored for 3 months at 37  C compared to control formulations (2-Vial, Liq, and POC) or unvaccinated mice. Reduction in CFUs in the (C) lungs and (D) spleens of mice immunized with lead candidate vaccine formulations stored for 3 months at 50  C compared to control formulations or unvaccinated mice. Mean and SD are indicated by black horizontal lines and gray vertical lines, respectively. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001 by one-way ordinary ANOVA, Welch's ANOVA, or Kruskal-Wallis tests depending on the distribution of the data, with corrections for multiple comparisons where selected pairwise comparisons included unvaccinated vs. all vaccine formulations, 2-Vial vs. three lead candidate formulations (heat-stressed), 2-Vial (heat-stressed) vs. three lead candidate formulations (heat-stressed), Liq (heat-stressed) vs. three lead candidate formulations (heat-stressed), and POC (heat-stressed) vs. three lead candidate formulations (heat-stressed).
Fig. 5

To determine the impact of storage at elevated temperatures on vaccine efficacy, mice were immunized intramuscularly on Study Day 0 and Study Day 21 with vaccine formulations that had been stored heat-stressed at 37  C or 50  C for 3 months. For comparison, control groups consisted of unvaccinated mice or mice vaccinated with heat-stressed POC, heat-stressed Liq, heat-stressed 2-Vial, or freshly prepared 2-Vial presentations. Four weeks following the second immunization, the mice were challenged with 50-100 CFUs of aerosolized Mtb (strain H37Rv). Four weeks following the Mtb exposure, bacterial burdens in the spleen and lung were quantified by the number of CFUs. Experiments were repeated once, with the combined results shown in Fig. 5. After storage for 3 months at 37  C, lead formulations TT and SP caused the greatest reductions in CFUs compared to unvaccinated and heat-stressed Liq, but CFU levels were not significantly different than the 2-Vial or POC controls (Fig. 5A and B). Greater differentiation in protective efficacy was apparent after storage of formulations for 3 months at 50  C. In particular, TT significantly reduced lung CFUs compared to unvaccinated, heat-stressed 2-Vial, and heat-stressed Liq (Fig. 5C), and significantly reduced spleen CFUs compared to unvaccinated mice (Fig. 5D). The magnitudes of CFU reduction shown here are consistent with previous experience regarding non-thermostable ID93 + GLA-SE and other vaccine compositions evaluated in similar mouse challenge models, where ~0.4-1 log reduction in lung CFUs was typically evident in immunized mice. Taken together, the efficacy data indicated TT offered the greatest level of protection among the lead formulations stored at elevated temperatures.
Discussion

Previous work that developed the three lead lyophilized TB vaccine candidate formulations demonstrated maintenance of physicochemical stability for 3 months at 37  C as well as maintenance of Th1-type immunogenicity responses in immunized mice after vaccine storage at 37  C or 50  C for 3 months. Here, with the motivation to obtain data enabling a down-selection to a single lead candidate formulation for advancement to clinical testing, morphology of the lyophilized and reconstituted formulations, short-term physicochemical stability when exposed to a range of alternative stress conditions, long-term physicochemical stability when stored at elevated temperatures for 58 months, and protective efficacy following thermal stress in a mouse challenge model were evaluated. While the three lead formulations appeared to have similar physical attributes as lyophilized cakes and reconstituted emulsions, the TT candidate was the most physicochemically stable formulation in the long-term temperature stability studies and retained the greatest biological activity in the protective efficacy studies. The alternative stress stability studies further differentiated the formulation candidates in nuanced ways and identified stresses of relevance for each formulation; for instance, the stress conditions to which TT was most susceptible were photochemical and oxidative but can potentially be mitigated through packaging interventions, such as filling into amber vials to reduce light exposure, or inert gas vial overlay and oxygen-free secondary packaging to reduce oxidation. Thus, only by considering the combination of physicochemical and biological data along with practical considerations was it possible to make a rational selection of the TT candidate as the lead single-vial lyophilized formulation of ID93 + GLA-SE for advanced development.

The comprehensive evaluation of multiple physicochemical and biological activity properties is not always reported in the literature for other thermostable adjuvanted subunit vaccine formulations. For instance, some reports describe a more limited testing approach, focusing only on selected readouts such as physical stability, in vivo immunogenicity, or in vitro antigenicity. However, relying solely on biological readouts is problematic since vaccine immunogenicity and/or efficacy in animal models may be largely retained even when substantial adjuvant or antigen content has been lost. For example, although most ID93 (antigen) and GLA (adjuvant component) content had been degraded in the single-vial liquid vaccine formulation (Liq) after storage for 3 months at 37  C (Fig. 4B and C), it still retained significant protective efficacy in terms of lung CFU reduction compared to unvaccinated mice (Fig. 5A). Since reduced amounts of ID93 and GLA still generated protective efficacy in the mouse challenge model, this particular readout by itself may be less discerning in evaluating effects of stability differences between formulations. It is unclear how similar losses in ID93 and GLA content would affect immune responses in humans. On the other hand, characterizing physical stability but not chemical stability may miss important changes. For instance, after storage of TT for 58 months at 50  C, relatively little change in emulsion particle size was evident even though most ID93 and GLA content had been lost (Fig. 5A-C). Thus, from a product development and quality control perspective, these findings underline the importance of characterizing multiple physical, chemical, and biological criteria to establish a complete stability profile of critical quality attributes.

A holistic data approach may also be useful to inform the establishment of product release and stability specifications. For instance, the high level of variation associated with the ID93 assay (Fig. 4C), combined with the knowledge that protective efficacy was retained even after significant ID93 loss (Fig. 5A), may indicate that a relatively wide specification range is appropriate for this component. Conversely, measurement of particle diameter demonstrates minimal variation between technical replicates, and little change in diameter was apparent in the lead candidate formulation even at extreme stress conditions, justifying a relatively narrow specification range for this attribute.

Although this study demonstrated a rational scientific approach for selecting a lead candidate formulation, additional practical factors should be considered in selecting a lead formulation for advanced development. For instance, different formulations may require different lyophilization process times (affecting efficiency and cost of production), some excipients may have sourcing limitations related to cost or availability while other excipients might be favored due to a long history of prior use in commercial products with well-established safety profiles, and some compositions may be associated with intellectual property considerations. In the present case, the TT lyophilization process was shorter than the SP lyophilization process, and although sucrose is more widely used in pharmaceutical products, pharmaceutical grade trehalose was available with no safety risks identified. Nevertheless, to reduce risk, an alternative back-up candidate should be identified (such as SP in the present report) in case advanced development challenges are encountered.

As expected, the stability trends first evident at 50  C generally foreshadowed the results obtained at later time points at the lower temperature of 37  C. However, the value of the short-term alternative stress stability data in predicting the long-term temperature stability performance was limited. For instance, after 58 months at 37  C, the TT candidate was the top performing formulation regarding the least change in particle diameter, ID93 content, and pH. However, only the short-term mechanical stress test indicated TT as a top performer with regards to particle diameter and ID93 content. As for GLA content, the TP candidate appeared to be the top performing formulation after 58 months at 37  C. Nevertheless, only the short-term oxidation stress test revealed TP as a top performer with regards to GLA content. These findings may reflect the difficulty in predicting stability of a complex vaccine composition with different instability mechanisms depending on the stress and the length of time that the stress is applied. Indeed, a limitation of the current work is that the specific degradation mechanisms and breakdown components of ID93 and GLA are not yet established. Future work in this regard is warranted as the vaccine advances through clinical development.
Conclusion

The physicochemical stability and protective efficacy of lead lyophilized formulation candidates of the ID93 + GLA-SE vaccine exposed to various stresses, including storage for nearly 5 years at elevated temperatures, were thoroughly evaluated using a suite of complementary techniques. Taken together, the combined data enabled selection of a lead candidate lyophilized formulation of ID93 + GLA-SE containing the disaccharide glass-forming excipient trehalose and Tris buffer. The lead formulation clearly demonstrated enhanced long-term thermostability compared to liquid formulation controls, including the current two-vial clinical presentation, and was considered suitable for future advanced development involving cGMP manufacturing and clinical testing.

passages.text: Newborn Screening for Fabry Disease: Current Status of Knowledge

Fabry disease is an X-linked progressive lysosomal disorder, due to alpha-galactosidase A deficiency. Patients with a classic phenotype usually present in childhood as a multisystemic disease. Patients presenting with the later onset subtypes have cardiac, renal and neurological involvements in adulthood. Unfortunately, the diagnosis is often delayed until the organ damage is already irreversibly severe, making specific treatments less efficacious. For this reason, in the last two decades, newborn screening has been implemented to allow early diagnosis and treatment. This became possible with the application of the standard enzymology fluorometric method to dried blood spots. Then, high-throughput multiplexable assays, such as digital microfluidics and tandem mass spectrometry, were developed. Recently DNA-based methods have been applied to newborn screening in some countries. Using these methods, several newborn screening pilot studies and programs have been implemented worldwide. However, several concerns persist, and newborn screening for Fabry disease is still not universally accepted. In particular, enzyme-based methods miss a relevant number of affected females. Moreover, ethical issues are due to the large number of infants with later onset forms or variants of uncertain significance. Long term follow-up of individuals detected by newborn screening will improve our knowledge about the natural history of the disease, the phenotype prediction and the patients' management, allowing a better evaluation of risks and benefits of the newborn screening for Fabry disease.
1. Introduction

Fabry disease (FD, OMIM 301500) is an X-linked lysosomal disorder, caused by alpha-galactosidase A (alpha-GalA) deficiency, encoded by GLA gene, that leads to progressive accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and related glycosphingolipids (Figure 1).

The clinical spectrum of FD is wide (Figure 2). Patients with a classic phenotype present with angiokeratomas, neuropathic pain, hypohidrosis, hearing loss and gastrointestinal symptoms. These symptoms can occur in early childhood before age 5 years, especially neuropathic pain and gastrointestinal symptoms. In adulthood, the patients can show severe involvement of kidney, heart, central nervous (mainly cerebrovascular disease) and peripheral nervous system. Patients presenting with the later onset subtypes have cardiac, renal and neurological involvements, with a different degree of clinical severity, in adulthood. The clinical manifestations in female heterozygotes also depend on the X-chromosome random inactivation that increases the phenotypic variability. Unlike other X-linked disorders, females with Fabry disease often show clinical manifestations. One possible explanation, besides X-inactivation and skew deviation, is the ineffective cross-correction of the enzyme activity in vivo. Unaffected fibroblasts from Fabry heterozygotes mostly secrete the mature form of the enzyme, which lacks the high-uptake mannose-6-phosphate residues. This form cannot be efficiently endocytosed by the affected cells. Therefore, a less active enzyme can complement the activity of the cells lacking expression of the enzyme.

The diagnosis can be confirmed by the enzyme activity measurement in dried blood spot (DBS), leukocytes, plasma or fibroblasts in FD males, identification of glycosphingolipid accumulation (Gb3 and especially its deacylated form lysoGb3 in plasma, urine, tissues) and genetic analysis. Several therapies are available: enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with recombinant human-galactosidase A (alfa 0.2 mg/kg or beta 1 mg/kg), to be given intravenously biweekly, and oral pharmacologic chaperon (migalastat) in patients with amenable pathogenic variants.
FD is a pan-ethnic disease, but a particularly high incidence of the later onset form is reported in Taiwan, due to the high prevalence of the pathogenic variant c.640-801G>A (IVS4+919G>A).

The therapy should be initiated as soon as possible on presentation of early signs. However, diagnostic delay is common, due to the heterogeneous and non-specific symptoms that frequently arise when organ damage is already irreversibly severe. In the absence of a detailed family history or in case of de novo variants, presymptomatic detection of FD can be achieved only through a newborn screening (NBS) program.

Here, we summarize the current state of newborn screening for FD, including our long-term experience. Finally, we give an overview of programs with some level of implementation worldwide, discuss these data and highlight advantages and limitations.
2. Methods

We searched PubMed and EMBASE until 28 February 2023, using the search terms "Fabry disease" and "newborn screening" or "Fabry disease" and "second tier test" or "newborn screening" and "lysoGb3". The search was extended with synonyms for FD and matching terms or headings. We selected full-text articles in peer reviewed journals in the English language. References were cross-checked for additional relevant papers.
3. Results
3.1. Screening Methods

From a technology perspective, high-throughput newborn screening for FD may be feasible using various analytical approaches (Table 1). Among these, the most frequently used are digital microfluidics (DMF) and tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), because they are multiplexable with commercially available reagents.

Immune quantification applies microbead array technology with detection of fluorescence to determine the amount of each protein. It requires protein-specific antibodies that are currently not commercially available. Moreover, the method is not useful in cases where a non-functional protein is produced.

Fluorometric enzymatic assay uses a fluorogenic substrate (4-methylumbelliferyl-D-galactopyranoside). After overnight incubation, the fluorescence of the enzyme product 4-MU (4-methylumelliferone) is measured.

DMF enzymatic assay is a multiplex approach, also based on fluorometric enzyme activity assays. Digital microfluidics involves the transport of sub-microliter volumes of both sample and enzyme assay components over an array of electrodes under the influence of an electric field, by a process known as electrowetting. The "spatial multiplexing" DMF method permits each LSD enzyme reactions to be performed in an individual droplet under its individually optimized conditions. It is the fastest currently available method, enabling same-day result reporting.

MS/MS enzymatic assay uses an assay mixture containing the substrate and internal standard. After overnight incubation, and remotion of detergents, salts and excess substrate, the samples are introduced to a tandem mass spectrometer. The enzymatic reaction product is quantified by determination of the ion abundance ratio of product to internal standard for each sample. Since all products and internal standards have different masses, several enzymes could be analyzed together by MS/MS.

Comparison between MS/MS and fluorometric method: DMF and MS/MS allow for the determination of multiple enzyme activities on a 3 mm disc-punch. Both use reagent kits supplied by commercial vendors (Babies Inc and Perkin-Elmer Life Sciences, respectively) that are inexpensive and readily available, but MS/MS, in contrast to DMF, can be modified by any laboratory to include more enzyme assays or other markers in a single assay. MS/MS assay needs overnight incubation and is performed in a 96-well format. DMF analyzes 40 samples within 4 h in 48-well cartridges. In an MS/MS assay, the pH is not optimized. For more enzymes that necessitate of different buffers, multiple incubations can be combined prior to a single injection into the mass spectrometer instrument, whereas with DMF, additional microfluidics cartridges and readers are required.
There are numerous reports claiming superior performance for MS/MS relative to fluorometry and DMF for LSD screening.

The superior analytical range of MS/MS compared to fluorometric assays has been described by several groups, providing a more accurate value of enzymatic activity, especially for very low values. This in turn predicts a lower number of screen positives. These data have been confirmed by retrospective comparative studies in Taiwan and USA. An additional advantage of MS/MS is that the substrates are closer in structure to the natural enzyme substrates, because incorporation of a fluorogenic group into the molecule is not required. Comparison of false positive rates is complicated by the fact that the values depend on the chosen cutoffs and by the uncertainty in establishing a positive sample based on gene sequencing (given the large numbers of variant of uncertain significance VUS). Probably the most important metric is the measured ratio of mean enzymatic activity of random newborns to that of affected samples. This ratio for MS/MS is 5- to 23-fold higher than that for DMFs, and it is expected to lead to a lower false positive rate. Precision studies carried out by the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Atlanta, GA, USA) in an identical setting and with identical samples show that MS/MS provides improved assay precision over DMF. However, a prospective comparative effectiveness study on 89,508 deidentified residual newborn DBS performed in California demonstrated that MS/MS, DMF and immunocapture showed high sensitivity, but lack in specificity, with need for improvement.
3.2. Second Tier Test

Specificity of the screening test can be improved with second tier biochemical or molecular testing. This latter is questionable because of the disclosure of genotypes associated with VUS and unclassified variants. Additionally, most NBS laboratories do not have the expertise to provide such second-tier testing.

As a biomarker, lysoGb3 can be measured in DBS by liquid chromatography-MS/MS technology. In patients with FD, the concentration of lysoGb3 has been shown to have diagnostic value, and it correlates with phenotype and severity of manifestations (high levels in patients with classic phenotype, especially male, mild-to-moderately elevated levels in individuals with later onset phenotype) and females. Moreover, it is a non-invasive marker for monitoring the disease during follow-up and treatment. There are a few reports in which lysoGb3 has been evaluated in the neonatal period. Increased values are very suggestive of FD, but normal lysoGb3 cannot exclude the possibility of later onset FD. In follow-ups of positive newborns with predicted later onset forms, the levels of lysoGb3 gradually increase with age, which might suggest a progressive and insidious accumulation. Thus, it may allow non-invasive investigation of patients in the presymptomatic period, despite it being yet unclear whether there is a critical threshold that justifies initiation of therapy.
3.3. Genetic Screening
Two molecular high-throughput methods, high-resolution melting analysis and Sequenom iPlex (Agena iPlex), have been investigated (Table 2).

High resolution melting (HRM) analysis: Primer sets were designed to cover the seven exons and the Asian common intronic pathogenic variant, IVS4+919G>A, of the GLA gene. The assay starts with PCR amplification in the presence of an appropriate DNA binding dye, followed by the formation of heteroduplex molecules and a final melting and analysis step. Variants are identified through a change in melting curve position, shape or deviated melting curve shape. Possible concerns may be the low sensitivity to identify all Fabry variants, especially those located at exons 2 and 6 because their amplicons are greater than 300 bp. The sensitivity to variable concentrations of nucleic acids or salts necessitates experience in analyzing the study results, because many parameters need periodic adjustment. Finally, HRM is not reliable for detecting male individuals, as the assay procedure depends on the formation of the heteroduplex.

Agena iPlex: It is a MassARRAY  genotyping platform that analyzes nucleotide variations by mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF), using a distinguishing allele-specific primer to amplify the extension products. Advantages of the Agena iPLEX assay are that stringent DNA quality control of the samples is not required, the procedure is relatively easy to perform in less than one day and the results can be interpreted by simply trained physicians and medical technologists. The limitation is that it only can detect known variants that have been designed into the assay panel. It is suitable when hotspot variants and common variations are known in a well-studied population. For example, in Taiwan, ~98% of Fabry patients carry variants out of a pool of only 21 pathogenic variants. An Agena iPLEX platform was designed to detect these 21 pathogenic variants and is being used.
3.4. Newborn Screening for FD in the World

Several NBS pilot studies and programs for FD have been implemented worldwide in recent years. However, state-based NBS programs still vary across countries, based on the economic cost of screening, local expertise and interest, political decisions and patient/family advocacy. A summary of available data on the reported NBS programs for FD is present in Table 3.

We reported the results from more than 5 years of NBS for FD in northeastern Italy, based on the determination of alpha-GalA enzyme activity in DBS using a multiplex MS/MS assay. Since 2015, 173,342 newborns (89,485 males) were screened. A genetic variant in the GLA gene (1:7879 newborns, 1:4068 males) was confirmed in 22 males. Among them, 13 carried a known pathogenic later onset variant (1:6883 males), and 9 had VUS or benign variants. The most common pathogenic variant was the later onset variant p.Asn215Ser (three patients). All patients were asymptomatic at the last follow-up (mean age 3 years), and none were receiving specific treatment. We did not detect any heterozygotes among the 83,853 newborn females screened.

Asia: In Taiwan, FD NBS started in 2006 using the fluorometric assay and then MS/MS. The prevalence of FD is very high in Taiwan. The IVS4+919G>A variant is the most common (82%, about 1 in 1600 males). This variant can activate an alternative splicing in intron 4, causing insertion of a 57-nucleotide sequence between exon 4 and 5 of the alphaGalA cDNA and subsequent premature termination after seven altered amino acid residues downstream from exon 4. This variant has been reported to be prevalently associated with cardiac involvement in FD, although a small portion of patients carrying this variant have clinical manifestations. Due to the low number of common pathogenic variants, and the high false negative rate in females (especially carrying IVS4 variant), a DNA-based NBS has been implemented (see above).
In Japan, enzyme-based pilot screening started in 2007, whereas in China only recently it has been introduced.

USA: FD was proposed for inclusion in the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP) in 2008. However, because of uncertainties about the NBS test's sensitivity, the prevalence of later onset variants, the unknown effectiveness of treatment and possible immunological response and the lack of prospective NBS and treatment studies, the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children (ACHDNC) rejected the proposal. However, local laws supported by NBS advocates and parents allowed the implementation of systemic screening for FD in several states. In 2013, Missouri became the first state to screen all newborns for multiple LSDs (including FD), using a DMF-based fluorescent assay. Within the first 6 months, 43,701 specimens were screened, and 15 newborns were reported to have a genetic diagnosis of FD (1:2913). In 2014, Illinois initiated a pilot screening program for five LSDs, including FD, using MS/MS, and it was followed by statewide screening in June 2015. Pilot studies and programs were then started in other states.

Europe: In Europe, the screening for LSDs is in its early stage. The first pilot study worldwide was conducted in 2003 in northern Italy using a fluorometric assay on 37,104 consecutive male newborns, and 12 of them were identified with FD (1 in 3100 males, of which 1 with a classic form). In Austria, a small pilot study was performed with almost 35,000 samples, using an MS/MS methodology, during which nine patients with FD were identified. There was also a pilot screening study in Hungary on about 40,000 samples using MS/MS, and three cases of FD were confirmed. A small pilot screening was also performed in Spain, with a high number of benign variants detected in confirmatory tests. The most relevant number of screened newborns in Europe was reported by our group in 2021 (see above).

These programs have demonstrated the feasibility of newborn screening for FD. It is difficult to make comparisons among studies because of the differences in screening techniques, the classification of later onset, benign variant and VUS, the cutoffs (usually more conservative at the start of the program), the numbers of screened newborns, the geographical/ethnical variation and the changes in the classification of variants over time as knowledge accumulates. While the positive predictive value (PPV, the fraction of test positives that are true positives) is the gold standard for evaluating medical tests, currently PPVs for NBS in FD cannot be used as a performance metric due to difficulty in the definition of true positives, because of the uncertainly in the onset of disease symptoms. In addition, the use of the false positive rate has the same problems. The only metric that can be reliably obtained is the ratio between the number of screen positives normalized to the number of newborns screened (the screen positive rate). This ratio can be used for prospective pilot studies, pilot studies with de-identified DBS and prospective NBS programs (PPV can only be obtained from live NBS programs). However, the rate of screen positives depends on the cutoff value chosen by each NBS laboratory.

Furthermore, disease incidence is only an estimate assuming that all "true positive" infants will develop symptoms. Moreover, most studies do not distinguish between male and female newborns, and these latter are lost to NBS. For example, a Spanish study reported a very high incidence of disease (1:394 births), but the number of screened newborns was relatively low (n = 14,600). Moreover, only 1 patient had a known pathogenic variant, while 25/37 carried benign variants. Different genetic backgrounds can also explain differences in incidence between countries. For example, in Taiwan, high incidence of the later onset GLA splicing variant (IVS4+919G>A) was detected. However, all studies showed that FD is surprisingly more prevalent than previously estimated (1:40,000 by Desnick et al.), especially the later onset form, which may represent an important unrecognized genetic disease.
3.5. Recommendations for Management of Positive Neonates

In most programs, if the alphaGalA activity is below the cutoff, the sample is retested (in duplicate), and, if the average of the duplicate persists below the cutoff, a second spot is requested. If the activity of the second spot is still below the cutoff, the infant is referred to the Clinic Unit for confirmatory testing. Samples are generally collected at a definite time in the first week of life, in several programs a second sample is required for premature babies (e.g., <34 gestational weeks and/or weight < 2000 g) and for sick newborns (e.g., those receiving transfusion or parenteral nutrition) or for samples with low activities for several enzymes due to a suspected preanalytical error.

Notably, different laboratories have different methods of determining cutoff values. Some laboratories use fixed cutoff values, established after the analysis of a set of normal control specimens. However, enzyme activity shows seasonal variation, related to the environmental temperature and humidity. Therefore, it is optimal to change the cutoff value for each test batch (e.g., % daily mean activity, DMA). Another method to identify suspected positive newborns is the use of postanalytical tools, such as Collaborative Laboratory Integrate Reports CLIR. This multivariate pattern recognition software compares each new case with disease and control profiles and determines a likelihood of disease score. It integrates all possible permutations of enzyme assay ratios (in multiplex assays) but also demographic information, such as age at specimen collection, birth weight and sex (that can impact white cell count and therefore enzyme activity). Sanders et al. demonstrated that CLIR tools markedly improves the performance of each NBS platform (false positive rates and PPVs).

Before the initiation of the NBS, protocols for definitive diagnostic tests, genetic counseling, follow up and treatment should be defined. Wang et al. developed guidelines for the diagnostic confirmation and management of presymptomatic individuals with lysosomal diseases, but more recent guidelines are lacking.

They suggested that once the diagnosis of FD has been confirmed, baseline diagnostic studies should be obtained. The infant should be seen by the metabolic specialist at 6-month intervals and monitored for onset of Fabry symptoms. For the individuals who have atypical variants, the strategy for regular follow-up and therapeutic intervention should be different from those with the classic type.

Gragnaniello et al. suggested that patients carrying variants associated with later onset forms should be monitored every 12 months, with clinical, instrumental and biochemical assessments. A suggested diagnostic and follow up algorithm for presymptomatic patients is presented in Table 4. However, further investigations are needed to find the optimal way for monitoring and treatment timing, especially for patients with unclassified, VUS and later onset variants. In part, the difficulty is due to the poor correlations of residual enzyme activity and genotype with the clinical phenotype. Long term follow-up programs will allow a better definition of natural history, management and response to therapies, providing answers to the many outstanding question.

An important aspect of the management of positive newborns is the family screening. The combination of a detailed pedigree analysis and cascade genetic testing of at-risk family members can increase the number of patients identified, improve early diagnosis and clarify the pathogenicity of novel GLA variants. In several studies it is reported that none of the infants with FD identified by NBS had a positive family history of FD or relatives with symptoms suggestive of the disease. However, when a family genetic screening was performed, all studied families had previously undiagnosed family members, symptomatic or not. Germain and the International Fabry Family Screening Advisory Board reviewed the literature on the family screening. For 365 probands, reported in 82 publications, 1744 affected family members were identified, which is equivalent to an average of 4.8 additional affected family members per proband. A similar number has also been reported in a US study. Potential barriers to the implementation of family genetic testing in some countries include associated costs, low awareness of its importance and cultural and societal issues.
3.6. Benefits and Challenges of FD Newborn Screening

In 1968, Wilson and Jungner described 10 principles that should be met prior to introducing a screening program. According to this algorithm, FD reaches a score of 8. Although the authors proposed a disease scoring >= 8.5 for consideration for NBS programs, it should be noted that most LSDs don't reach this threshold. Thus, the implementation of FD newborn screening is still controversial.
Advantages and disadvantages of the FD newborn screening are summarized in Table 5.

As discussed above, reliable and effective methods for screening on DBS are available. The disease is more prevalent than previously clinically estimated. Newborn screening allows the early diagnosis and treatment, leading to a better prognosis. Moreover, the diagnosis of a newborn can be followed by family counselling and screening.

Later onset forms: The high incidence of later onset forms has raised ethical issues. Detection in the newborn period may have a negative psychological impact on parents and carries the risk to create "vulnerable children" or "patients in waiting", labelled and overmedicated. Moreover, it increases the costs for diagnostic laboratory testing and follow-up visits. The long-term follow-up of these infants will be essential to understand the natural history of the disease (which includes the manifestations of the different phenotypes) and the impact of early treatment. However, an early diagnosis of the later onset forms may have several advantages. A significant number of patients currently remain mis- or undiagnosed for many years. The implementation of NBS could avoid this "diagnostic odyssey", allowing timely treatment and subsequently better outcome. Moreover, their identification allows physicians to perform cascade genotyping in at risk family members and identify undiagnosed relatives.

VUS/benign variants: NBS revealed a high incidence of polymorphisms, e.g., p.Asp313Tyr in European population and p.Glu66Gln in Japan, that are considered to be non-pathogenic based on in vitro expression, lysoGb3 concentrations in plasma, prevalence in healthy alleles and clinical and histological features.

Screening for FD also reveals a high prevalence of individuals with VUS or novel not yet classified genetic variants. To determine whether these variants were pathogenic or not, functional (e.g., in vitro analysis, in silico tools), biochemical (e.g., lysoGb3), pedigree analyses and especially clinical manifestations should be performed and often many years are needed to correctly classify a variant. For example, in Caucasian newborns, the most frequent genetic alteration reported is p.Ala143Thr. Although it has been reported in association with both classic and later onset (renal and cardiac) FD, it has been recently suggested to be a benign variant. Study in COS cells demonstrated a high residual enzyme activity of 36%. Reported individuals with this variant showed unspecific symptoms, but no increase of plasma Gb3 and LysoGb3 and no storage in tissue biopsies. The high incidence of this variant in gnomAD database (5.06 x 10-4) and in the screening programs supports its lack of pathogenicity. Furthermore, the alphaGalA enzyme is localized within the lysosome, suggesting normal trafficking. Therefore, the pathogenicity of this variant is still debatable.

Female newborns: Enzymatic tests are not reliable for screening females due to random X-inactivation in different tissues. False negative results with enzymatic assays are about 40% (up to 80% in Taiwan, where the IVS4 variant is predominant), whereas DNA-based methods appear to be more sensitive and reliable. In most countries, mutational heterogeneity hampers the use of molecular analysis for high-throughput screening. Nevertheless, genetic assays may be considered in the near future, specifically due to improved technologies.

NBS cannot accurately distinguish classic from later onset forms: The prediction of disease severity is difficult, because enzyme activity and genotype do not clearly correlate with the phenotype and there is a large number of private GLA variants. Moreover, the influence of modifier genes or other genetic factors on phenotype severity may be confounding, since individuals with the same GLA variant may occasionally have variable clinical manifestations during disease progression. For heterozygotes, lyonization makes presymptomatic prediction of phenotypic severity impossible. The only test that seems to predict a classic form on NBS is lysoGb3 measurement (elevated), but, as discussed above, it cannot accurately differentiate the different forms.

Ideally FD NBS program should include: (1) a combined enzymatic and genetic approach, to perform a complete screening of all patients (males and females), and the enzymatic and genetic approach would be complementary in supporting the difficult interpretation of genetic variants; (2) an improved biomarker to use as second tier test. At the moment we do not have an ideal disease-specific biomarker for Fabry disease. Plasma lysoGb3 has been established as a good diagnostic biomarker for Fabry disease. Nevertheless, lysoGb3 is not highly sensitive and highly specific as lysoGb1 for NBS in Gaucher disease. LysoGb3 correlates well with the classic form, male sex, but normal levels cannot rule out a later-onset form. Furthermore, most of the literature regarding lysoGb3 refers to measurements in adult Fabry patients, and we need more data on values during infancy; (3) a newborn screening program for FD should be associated with a long-term follow-up program. Indeed, only such a clinical follow-up could determine the impact of this early diagnosis in the real-life management.

However, despite these limitations, the opinion of FD patients about NBS is favorable. Several studies explored the opinion of FD patients (n = 88) on NBS for FD (and other later onset diseases). Most participants agree with NBS. They felt NBS could result in better current health, eliminate diagnostic odysseys, lead to more timely and efficacious treatment and lead to different life-decision, including lifestyle, financial and reproductive decisions. A different opinion is reported by genetic healthcare providers. Indeed, Lisi et al. evaluated the opinion of 38 genetic healthcare providers: FD was viewed less favorable that other LSDs due to later age of onset (potential for medicalization, stigmatization and psychological burden) and ambiguity regarding prognosis.
4. Conclusions and Future Directions
The lack of a second-tier test suitable to cover all the forms of the disease and reduce the recall rate;
No biochemical detection of heterozygous females;
The clinical interpretation of unclassified variants and VUS;
The impact of early diagnosis on patients with later onset forms.
The frequency and technical practicability make NBS for FD feasible and affordable to be extended to large population. However, several issues still need further study:

Efforts to capture long term follow-up data, associated to functional characterization of the controversial variants, studies of biomarkers and modifier genes to a better phenotype prediction and patients' management will be crucial to address important ethical issues. To conclude, both the benefits and risks of NBS merit further study, underscoring the need for long term follow up.

passages.text: Multiplexing Iduronate-2-Sulphatase (MPS-II) into a 7-Plex Lysosomal Storage Disorder MS/MS Assay Using Cold-Induced Phase Separation

Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (MPS-II, Hunter syndrome, OMIM:30990) is a lysosomal storage disorder (LSD) that results in iduronate 2-sulphatase (I2S) enzyme deficiency. MPS-II was added to the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP) in August 2022; thus, there is an increased demand for multiplexing I2S into existing LSD screening assays. After incubation with LSD synthetic substrates, extracts are cleaned using liquid-liquid extraction with ethyl acetate or protein precipitation using acetonitrile (ACN). We investigated cold-induced water ACN phase separation (CIPS) to improve the combination of 6-plex and I2S extracts to create a 7-plex assay, and compared it to room temperature ACN and ethyl acetate liquid-liquid extraction. The extracts were dried and resuspended in the mobile phase, and then analyzed using an optimized 1.9 min injection-to-injection liquid chromatography method coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). The combination of ACN and CIPS improved the detection for I2S products without significant detriment to other analytes, which is attributable to a more complete coagulation and separation of heme, proteins, and extracted residual salts. Using CIPS for sample cleanup in dried blood spots (DBS) appears to represent a promising and straightforward way of achieving cleaner sample extracts in a new 7-plex LSD screening panel.
1. Introduction

Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (MPS-II, Hunter syndrome, OMIM:30990) is a lysosomal storage disorder (LSD) that results in iduronate 2-sulphatase (I2S) enzyme deficiency. MPS-II was added to the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP) in August 2022; thus, there is an increased demand to multiplex I2S in existing LSD screening assays. LSD newborn screening is mandated by many states in the United States. Although there are dozens of LSDs, current assays often include Pompe disease (added to RUSP in 2013) and mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS-I, added to RUSP in 2018), with many laboratories working towards the inclusion of MPS-II. These disorders all stem from insufficient lysosomal enzymatic activity, leading to a build-up of macromolecules that are not properly catabolized. This results in the inappropriate accumulation and storage of complex carbohydrates, glycosaminoglycans, and lipids.

Current LSD platforms in newborn screening include fluorescence-based methods and tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) with sample introduction using flow injection analysis (FIA) or liquid chromatography (LC). Researchers have attempted to create a 7-plex assay (i.e., screening for seven LSDs in parallel using MS/MS in a single assay); however, structural similarity between substrates for I2S and alpha-L-iduronidase (IDUA) results in the cross-reactivity of the I2S substrate with IDUA. Therefore, producing a true 7-plex assay that is capable of screening all disorders from a single dried blood spot (DBS) punch is challenging. Instead, current methods focus on I2S as a stand-alone assay (1-plex), and extracts from 6-plex assays (i.e., MPS-I, Pompe, Gaucher, Fabry, Krabbe, and Niemann-Pick A/B disorders) and a 1-plex I2S assay are combined downstream after the enzymes are inhibited. (2) Following the punching of DBS, incubation takes place in an aqueous, highly buffered solution using non-volatile salts that extract high amounts of proteins. This extract is not compatible with downstream liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis, so an additional cleanup step is required. There are currently two approaches used. The most common uses liquid-liquid extraction with ethyl acetate (EtOAc), which quenches the reaction and eliminates salts and proteins. The second approach uses acetonitrile (ACN) at room temperature (RT-ACN) for quenching and protein precipitation, with the extract from the top of the sample wells being transferred for analysis after centrifugation. Both approaches have drawbacks. The water:EtOAc liquid-liquid extraction method leads to a very clean extract, but suffers from the low recovery of analytes of interest, such as enzymatic products and internal standards (IS). ACN addition alone effectively precipitates the proteins and recovers more product, but recovers a high amount of salts that can be detrimental to the robustness of the LC-MS/MS assay.

Miscible mixtures of water with ACN can be phase-separated using either kosmotropic salts or by decreasing the temperature to around -17  C, the latter being coined as cold-induced aqueous ACN phase separation (CIPS). CIPS causes true phase layers to form (Figure 1), creating a liquid-liquid extraction that separates unwanted materials from the desired sample. This performs the same function as the layers formed by the EtOAc method, but reduces the method's overall complexity and the risk posed to the analyst from EtOAc. This study investigates the use of CIPS to improve the combination of 6-plex and 1-plex extracts to increase the recovery of analytes of interest and eliminate non-volatile salts, while improving the robustness and throughput of the assay. To our knowledge, this is the first reported use of CIPS in a newborn screening assay.
2. Materials and Methods

All product information and sources (i.e., solvents, consumables, etc.) are presented in Supplemental Table S1. The DBS analyzed for this study were produced using a base pool of double leuko-depleted blood and three enriched levels using cord blood to produce 0, 5, 50, and 100% relative enzyme activity pools. Samples were 3.2 mm DBS punches taken from LSD quality control (QC) materials (Lot 2108), from levels A (0%) through to D (100%). The enzyme substrates, internal standards (S&IS), and buffers were purchased from PerkinElmer  as LSD 6-plex S&ISs and 1-plex I2S S&ISs. A list of enzymes and quantification m/z ions is available in Table 1.

6-plex and 1-plex S&ISs were resuspended using 21 mL of the corresponding buffer per vial. Two identical 96-well plates were prepared for each sample run, with 40 microL of 6-plex S&IS per well in one and 40 microL of 1-plex S&IS per well in the other. The plates were heat-sealed with foil, centrifuged for 30 s to ensure DBS coverage, and incubated at 37  C for 18 h. RT-ACN quenching steps and EtOAc washing were performed, according to previously reported methods.

For the CIPS ACN quench, 200 microL of -20  C ACN was added to each sample well in both the 6-plex and 1-plex plates. The solution was mixed 10 times with a pipette, and the plate was resealed with foil, centrifuged for 1 min at 3500 rpm, and placed in a -20  C freezer for 12 min. In this study, all CIPS sample upper layers were transferred within 2 min of removal from the freezer. The low temperature caused the ACN and aqueous contents to separate, forming an ACN-enriched upper layer containing the enzyme products and an aqueous-enriched bottom layer containing excess salts, heme, and proteins. After removing both plates (i.e., 6-plex and 1-plex) from the freezer, 75 microL was transferred from the ACN layer to a fresh plate and combined with corresponding sample extracts from the other plate, creating a total volume 150 uL of extracts from both plates in a new 96-well plate. The combined extracts were dried for 10 min under N2 gas at 50  C with flow rates of 50 L/min upper and 20 L/min lower, and then resuspended in 150 microL of 30% ACN, 70% water, and a 0.1% formic acid solution. The samples were shaken at RT for 10 min in a sealed plate prior to injection.

The samples were analyzed on a Waters  Xevo TQD using LC-MS/MS with a Acquity  XSelect CSH 1.7 microm x 2.1 mm x 50 mm UPLC column and the corresponding 5 mm guard column. Mobile Phase A was comprised of 20% ACN, 80% water, and 0.01% formic acid. Mobile Phase B was comprised of 70% ACN, 30% methanol, and 0.01% formic acid. Weak wash was comprised of 50% water and 50% ACN, and strong wash was 100% ACN. The LC-MS gradient ran from 75%A:25%B to 1%A:99%B from 0 to 1.10 min at a flow rate of 0.790 mL/min, with all analytes eluting by 1.2 min (Figure 2). The column was washed for 15 s before injection and 25 s after injection. The column was heated at 60  C during the analysis. The method's total turnaround time for each sample was 1.9 min.

Enzyme activity is typically calculated using the following equation: where M1 is the peak area of the product, M2 is the peak area of the IS, [IS] is the concentration of the IS solution for the analyte, VIS is the volume of the IS solution added at incubation (40 microL), VDBS is the estimated volume of blood contained in the DBS punch (3.1 microL), and T is the time of incubation. Note that IS solutions were prepared at a different concentration for this assay than what is typically standard. We presented the effects of CIPS on M2 (from Equation (1)) to demonstrate how IS recoveries are significantly impacted by sample workup. Since ISs are isotopically labeled versions of the enzymatic products, we chose to present only IS data for brevity purposes. Enzyme products demonstrated similar phase affinities. The IS data from the DBS-extracted samples were used to account for matrix effects during the comparison stage. The raw MS data were imported into Waters  TargetLynx (V4.2) to obtain the peak areas, and were imported into the open-source software Skyline (V 20.1.0.155) for visualization purposes.
3. Results

The peak areas for all IS and analytes were significantly higher for RT-ACN and CIPS methods compared to the EtOAc method (Figure 3). For I2S and IDUA, peak areas for the IS and product were below 1000 counts when using EtOAc, and slightly higher with the CIPS method than with RT-ACN. GLA and GAA also showed a strong affinity for ACN-based separations, with slight increases in peak areas with CIPS and comparable product recoveries.
4. Discussion

Further method optimization is in progress for multiple method steps. CIPS requires the samples to be at low temperatures during the organic phase separation process, and since fewer samples imply lower thermal capacity, the time it takes for the samples to warm is related to the number of samples on the 96-well plate. Using two minutes as the time to transfer in this study was determined to be a safe option in order to reduce potential plate-to-plate variability in our laboratory. This time may vary with ambient temperatures, the number of samples on each plate, and handling procedures. The use of a cold base plate chiller upon removing CIPS samples from the freezer can extend the time buffer for the top layer transfer. Continued minor adjustments to the chromatographic method will be made to improve analyte peak resolution and separation.

The recommended S&IS concentrations from the flow injection analysis (FIA)-MS/MS LSD 6-plex assay are higher than those required for this LC-MS assay. The chromatographic separation of enzyme products causes less ion suppression, improving the assay's sensitivity. Reducing the concentration of S&IS for this assay led to improved peak shapes and baseline resolution for analytes that need to be separated. While the method separates the substrate from the product in all cases, there is an observable risk of column saturation and loss of baseline resolution between these peaks when using higher concentrations of S&IS. Based on the aforementioned issues and preliminary data from our pilot studies, we used the provided buffer to resuspend S&IS vials at 21 mL instead of at 3.3 mL. We observed sufficient signals for all analytes at this concentration with improved peak shapes.

Our study improves upon the existing methods for sample preparation and LC-MS/MS analysis for LSD biomarkers. The product and IS recovery are 2.5-60 times higher with CIPS than with EtOAc (Figure 3), depending on the enzyme. CIPS requires fewer handling steps and smaller wash volumes, reducing the potential for operator errors in pipette mixing and transfer steps, along with product loss. There is a distinct benefit to adding CIPS to ACN methods, and analyte recovery is comparable or slightly improved for all analytes between the CIPS and RT-ACN methods. Since the separation of heme, proteins, and excess aqueous layer salts is more complete with CIPS than with RT-ACN alone, the robustness of the assay is improved. This method also reduces the time required to analyze each sample when compared to previously published methods that can screen for MPS II and is similar to FIA methods. This LC-MS/MS-based LSD 7-plex assay is a high-throughput and cost-effective method to add screening for MPS-II to the newborn screening panel.
